## Publications

::: {.pub}
[Party Politics · 2026 · OnlineFirst]{.kicker}

[[Bureaucratic appointments and coalition support in presidential systems: An analysis of Brazil's Chamber of Deputies](https://doi.org/10.1177/13540688261466129){target="_blank" .no-arrow}]{.pub-title}

[Osamura, K.]{.meta}

<details class="more">
<summary>Summary</summary>

Presidents in multiparty systems keep coalition partners on board not only with ministries but also with lower-level posts in the bureaucracy. Using roll-call votes on 161 bills in Brazil's Chamber of Deputies (2003–2018), I show that these appointments strongly increase legislative support for the government's bills.

</details>
:::

## Dissertation

::: {.boxes .stacked}
::: {.box}
[Seeking Office, Policy, or Votes? An Analysis of Legislative Coalitions, Motivations, and Behavior in Multiparty Presidential Systems]{.box-title}

<!-- [Defended on 22 September 2026 at the University of Vienna]{.meta} -->

[**Supervision:** Prof. Thomas M. Meyer, PhD, and Prof. Dr. Laurenz Ennser-Jedenastik]{.meta}

[**Committee:** Chair: Prof. Markus Wagner (Vienna); External examiners: Prof. Timothy J. Power (Oxford), Assoc. Prof. Thiago Nascimento da Silva (Australian National University)]{.meta}

<details class="more">
<summary>Summary</summary>

Most research on coalitions in presidential systems focuses on the president who builds them. My dissertation looks instead at the parties that join, stay in, or leave these governments, and at what they seek: office, policy, or votes. Three papers take each goal in turn, studying political appointments in Brazil, ideological distance and law-making in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile, and the electoral fate of legislators who break with their party in Brazil and Chile.

</details>
:::
:::
